question: What defines rational drug use for a patient?

options.A: Buying the most expensive brand name drugs on the market
options.B: Taking every available drug to speed up recovery time
options.C: Receiving the right medicine for their specific clinical need
options.D: Stopping medication immediately after symptoms disappear

explanation: Rational drug use requires matching the correct drug therapy to the specific clinical diagnosis of the individual patient. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T9#GNS223_U3_T9_h1)

question: Why is the nurse considered the final safety checkpoint in drug administration?

options.A: Nurses write the original drug orders on patient charts
options.B: Nurses verify prescriptions before administering drugs to patients
options.C: Nurses have the legal authority to manufacture hospital drugs
options.D: Nurses decide the retail price of medications in pharmacies

explanation: The nurse checks the medication order and patient status right before administration, catching errors before they reach the patient. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T9#GNS223_U3_T9_h1)

question: The WHO principle of appropriate indication means what for the patient?

options.A: The drug must have a pleasant taste for easy swallowing
options.B: A valid medical reason must exist for taking the drug
options.C: The medication must be manufactured in a local facility
options.D: The patient must be able to afford the medication cost

explanation: Appropriate indication ensures drugs are only prescribed when a clear, medically justified reason demands treatment. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T9#GNS223_U3_T9_h2)

question: What happens when the WHO principle of appropriate dose is ignored?

options.A: The medication shelf life extends past the expiration date
options.B: The patient automatically develops a lifelong allergy
options.C: The drug manufacturer will recall the product from shelves
options.D: Toxicity or treatment failure may occur in the patient

explanation: Incorrect dosing either fails to treat the condition or causes dangerous drug accumulation leading to toxicity. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T9#GNS223_U3_T9_h2)

question: What is polypharmacy?

options.A: The simultaneous use of multiple medications by a patient
options.B: The manufacturing of fake drugs in unlicensed factories
options.C: The practice of buying drugs from unregistered market vendors
options.D: The storage of expired medicines in a home cupboard

explanation: Polypharmacy refers to taking multiple medications concurrently, which raises the risk of adverse interactions. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T9#GNS223_U3_T9_h3)

question: Why does incomplete antibiotic treatment contribute to antimicrobial resistance?

options.A: Stronger bacteria survive the low drug levels and multiply
options.B: The patient's immune system stops recognizing normal bacteria
options.C: Expired chemicals turn into harmless water inside the body
options.D: The remaining pills in the pack attract dangerous fungi

explanation: Stopping antibiotics early leaves hardy bacteria alive, allowing them to multiply and resist future treatments. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T9#GNS223_U3_T9_h3)

question: When should nurses perform medication reconciliation for hospitalized patients?

options.B: At the end of every calendar month
options.C: Only when the patient requests a drug refill
options.D: Every hour during routine vital sign checks

explanation: Medication reconciliation must happen at every transition of care to catch discrepancies and prevent errors. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T9#GNS223_U3_T9_h4)

question: A patient admits to taking orthodox blood pressure drugs alongside local herbal teas. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Throw away the herbal tea without telling the attending physician
options.B: Scold the patient for mixing traditional mixtures with modern medicine
options.C: Prescribe a higher dose of the blood pressure medication immediately
options.D: Document the herbal use and report potential interactions to the team

explanation: The nurse must document all substances taken and communicate potential herb-drug interactions to the multidisciplinary team. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T9#GNS223_U3_T9_h4)

question: Why do complex dosing schedules often lead to poor medication adherence?

options.A: Complex schedules cause medications to expire inside the packaging
options.B: Patients easily become confused and forget when to take doses
options.C: Insurance companies charge extra fees for complicated regimens
options.D: Pharmacies refuse to dispense drugs with multiple daily instructions

explanation: Simpler dosing schedules make it easier for patients to remember their medications and stick to the treatment plan. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T9#GNS223_U3_T9_h5)

question: What is a practical nursing strategy to help a forgetful patient remember their medications?

options.A: Using pill organizers or setting alarm reminders
options.B: Hiding the medication bottles in a secure locked cabinet
options.C: Stopping the medication until memory improves naturally
options.D: Doubling the morning dose to make up for missed pills

explanation: Practical memory aids like pill boxes and alarms assist patients in taking their drugs at the scheduled times. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T9#GNS223_U3_T9_h5)

question: What is the primary goal of pharmacovigilance in clinical practice?

options.B: Lowering the market price of imported pharmaceuticals
options.C: Increasing the manufacturing speed of local drugs
options.D: Detecting and preventing adverse drug effects

explanation: Pharmacovigilance focuses on monitoring, understanding, and preventing harmful reactions linked to pharmaceutical products. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T9#GNS223_U3_T9_h6)

question: Why is reporting adverse drug reactions to NAFDAC important for public health?

options.A: It helps track unsafe products and prevents widespread harm
options.B: It guarantees financial compensation for affected patients
options.C: It eliminates the need for doctors to write prescriptions
options.D: It forces pharmaceutical companies to close down permanently

explanation: National regulatory reporting allows authorities to identify safety signals and protect the wider public from dangerous drugs. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T9#GNS223_U3_T9_h6)

question: What is the main purpose of hospital antibiotic stewardship programs?

options.A: To speed up the discharge process for surgical patients
options.B: To curb antimicrobial resistance through careful prescribing
options.C: To ensure hospitals only buy the most expensive antibiotics
options.D: To ban the use of all injectable medications in wards

explanation: Antibiotic stewardship programs monitor and optimize antibiotic use to prevent the rise of resistant pathogen strains. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T9#GNS223_U3_T9_h7)

question: Which group of professionals should collaborate closely on hospital wards to review drug charts?
explanation: Nurses and clinical pharmacists working together can catch prescribing errors and optimize patient medication regimens. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T9#GNS223_U3_T9_h7)
